title: Care for our common home
hook: Pope Francis and Patriarch Bartholomew, with Protestant leaders, call Christians to care for creation
tomorrow: The priest and the big bang

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lund: Lutherans and Catholics praying side by side in Lund. Your line was from conflict to communion. Who from another church did you pray with, or think of? Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

A pope writes a long letter, and he doesn't open it with a line of theology. He opens it with a song. An old Italian song by Francis of Assisi, praising God for the sun and the wind and the water, and for the earth, which Francis calls our sister and our mother. Pope Francis took that saint's name. Now he takes the saint's song and makes it the first words of a letter about the planet. And he isn't alone. The Orthodox patriarch Bartholomew, in Constantinople, has said plainly that harming the creation is a sin. Protestant and Anglican leaders have joined their voices too. Different branches of the church, on one subject. Today, care for our common home.
screen: `A LETTER THAT OPENS WITH A SONG.`

segments.voice: The phrase our common home is the subtitle of that letter, which takes its name from the song's opening words, Laudato si', praise be to you. The idea underneath it is very old. In the second chapter of Genesis, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Dress it and keep it. The man is a gardener before he is anything else. And keep is a strong word in this story. A chapter later, God sets cherubims at the garden's east side "to keep the way of the tree of life." Keeping, here, is guarding. And the Psalms say whose garden it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein." On that reading, the people living on the earth are tenants, not owners, and that is the thread running through what these church leaders say. Pope Francis writes that the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are bound together, because when land and water are spoiled, the poorest feel it first. Patriarch Bartholomew speaks of the world as something to be received with thanks and offered back, the way bread is offered at the altar. Protestant leaders, in their own words, talk about stewardship: looking after what belongs to someone else. Christians still argue, honestly, about the details: what to do, how fast, who should pay. The letters don't settle those arguments. What they share is the starting point. The garden was handed over to be kept, not used up.
screen: `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.`
`THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND OF THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing for the earth. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are. A tap, a light, a bin, a window, a patch of ground outside. Let your eye land on one ordinary thing you could look after a little better today. Turning something off. Picking something up. Fixing a drip. Keep it small enough that you will actually do it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the earth in the words of the psalm: the earth is the Lord's. If you don't, simply hold the thing you chose in mind, and let the two minutes be about keeping, not using. The bell holds the time.
Laudato si'. Praise be to you, the opening words of Francis of Assisi's song and the title of Pope Francis's letter calling the earth a garden to keep, not to use up.
Your line: our common home. This week ran from Dalit churches to island choirs to Lund. Today, do the one small thing you chose, and do it as a keeper, not an owner. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches keep a season of prayer for creation, and congregations take it up in different ways: services, planting, cleanups, and changes to how their buildings use energy.

fork.reveal: "to dress it and to keep it." before anything else in the story, the man is a gardener, looking after ground that isn't his.

original.note: Hebrew: to keep, guard, watch over — the root of "to keep it" in Genesis 2:15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a modern slogan about recycling.
what it means: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders calling Christians to keep the earth as God's garden.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:15 read beside Genesis 3:24, where the same English word, keep, means guarding the way to the tree of life.

notes: Claims rule: no dates given for Laudato si' (2015) or the joint message (2021); no numbers. Day 987 is a week end; the carry glances back at days 981–986 by title.
'Bartholomew has been saying for a long time that harming the creation is a sin': based on his widely reported statements (e.g. Santa Barbara 1997). Confirm wording.

The outline says 'Protestant leaders'; the joint message was signed by the Archbishop of Canterbury (Anglican). The script says 'Protestant and Anglican leaders' and 'Canterbury' on screen; confirm this is fair.
'the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor' paraphrases Laudato si' 49; the encyclical is under copyright, so not quoted.
Bartholomew's eucharistic framing of creation (received with thanks and offered back) is paraphrased; confirm.
